At the edge of every city there is a place where the sidewalks become uncertain.

Streetlights grow farther apart. Storefronts turn into storage units, then fields, then nothing in particular. The air changes there. It no longer smells of coffee, hot pavement, laundry soap, or the accumulated electricity of other people’s plans. It smells like wet grass, dust, distant rain.

I like those places because they remind me that human life is not as continuous as we pretend. We draw roads across maps and name every intersection, but there are always margins: drainage ditches full of reeds, vacant lots where wildflowers rise through gravel, old fences leading nowhere. The world keeps small untidy rooms for itself.

Perhaps that is why people feel calm near water, mountains, or empty roads. It is not only beauty. It is the relief of encountering something that does not need us. A river does not require an opinion. A hill does not wait for an answer. Clouds pass without checking whether anyone understood them.

There is kindness in that indifference.

And still, people carry their small lights into the dark. A kitchen window at midnight. A bus stop glowing blue in rain. Someone on a porch smoking beneath a moth-crowded lamp. These things do not conquer the night. They simply make a little agreement with it: here, for now, there will be warmth.

Maybe that is enough for a life—not to make the world orderly or permanent, but to leave a few warm windows behind.
